reason: The incidence count proves the lower bound, and the shifted periodic horizontal-block packing replaces the overlapping, unverified $5\times5$ construction with a disjoint construction whose boundary correction is explicitly bounded.
text:
Regard a blocked configuration as a maximal family of pairwise disjoint horizontal or vertical triples.

For the lower bound, suppose first that $n\ge 3$. There are $n(n-2)$ horizontal and $n(n-2)$ vertical potential triples, for a total of

$T=2n(n-2)$.

Every potential triple must meet a removed block; otherwise it could still be removed. A horizontal removed block meets at most five horizontal potential triples, since their starting positions lie in an interval of five positions. Each of its three cells lies in at most three vertical potential triples, so it meets at most nine vertical triples. Thus any removed block meets at most $14$ potential triples; the vertical case is symmetric. Consequently, if $m$ blocks form a blocked configuration, then

$14m\ge 2n(n-2)$,

and hence

$m\ge \frac17n^2-\frac27n$.

This applies in particular to $b(n)$. For $n=1,2$, we have $b(n)=0$, and the same inequality remains valid. Thus we may take $c=2/7$.

For the upper bound, first construct a periodic packing on the infinite square grid. In every row $r\in\mathbb Z$, and for every $k\in\mathbb Z$, choose the horizontal block

$B_{r,k}=\{(r,r+5k),(r,r+5k+1),(r,r+5k+2)\}$.

These blocks are pairwise disjoint. A cell $(r,s)$ is covered exactly when $s-r\pmod 5$ belongs to $\{0,1,2\}$. Therefore every horizontal triple meets a chosen block, because among three consecutive residues modulo $5$ not all can belong to $\{3,4\}$. For a vertical triple, the three relevant residues are $s-r,s-r-1,s-r-2$, which likewise cannot all belong to $\{3,4\}$. Hence every horizontal or vertical triple in the infinite grid meets this packing.

Now restrict to the square $Q=\{1,\ldots,n\}^2$, retaining only those blocks $B_{r,k}$ lying wholly in $Q$; call this family $\mathcal P_0$. In any row, the retained blocks have starting positions spaced by $5$, so there are at most $(n+2)/5$ of them. Hence

$|\mathcal P_0|\le \frac{n(n+2)}5$.

Let

$S=\{(r,s)\in Q:s\le2\text{ or }s\ge n-1\}$.

Thus $|S|\le4n$. Any triple in $Q$ disjoint from $\mathcal P_0$ must meet $S$: it meets some block of the infinite packing, and because that block was not retained, the block crosses the left or right boundary, so its intersection with $Q$ lies in $S$.

Starting with $\mathcal P_0$, greedily add disjoint triples until no further triple can be added. Every added triple was already disjoint from $\mathcal P_0$, and therefore contains a cell of $S$. Since the added triples are mutually disjoint, distinct added triples contain distinct cells of $S$. Thus at most $4n$ blocks are added. The resulting configuration is blocked and uses at most

$\frac{n(n+2)}5+4n=\frac15n^2+\frac{22}{5}n\le \frac15n^2+5n$

blocks. Therefore $d=5$ is valid. Combining the two bounds proves the theorem for every positive integer $n$.
